{"answers":[{"question_id":"Q022_colg_crya_remote_homology","answer":"SCOPe changed these domains from separately classified structures to inferred remote homologues. The API identifies current SCOPe as 2.08, with latest periodic update 2.08-2026-08-16.

In SCOPe 2.04, the ColG collagen-binding domain in 1nqd (d1nqda_, SUNID 86025) belonged to family b.23.2.1 and superfamily b.23.2, both named Collagen-binding domain, within the CUB-like fold b.23. Cry3A’s C-terminal domain in 1dlc (d1dlca1, SUNID 23719; chain A residues 500–644) belonged to the delta-Endotoxin, C-terminal domain family b.18.1.3, within the Galactose-binding domain-like superfamily b.18.1 and fold b.18. They shared only the All beta proteins class b; that classification did not assert common ancestry, although it did not rule it out.

In current SCOPe, ColG has moved to family b.18.1.36 (SUNID 267607), whereas Cry3A remains b.18.1.3 (SUNID 49796). Both now share superfamily b.18.1 (SUNID 49785) and fold b.18 (SUNID 49784). Thus, SCOPe recognizes probable common ancestry at the superfamily level while retaining distinct families; this is stronger than merely recognizing a similar fold.

The structural support concerns their corresponding beta-sandwich cores and strand topology. SCOPe describes the shared fold as a two-sheet, nine-strand jelly-roll. Its ColG-family annotation explicitly cites PMID 17977833 for likely homology connecting ColG (d1nqdb_), the Cry4Ba C-terminal domain (d1w99a3), and the Clostridium perfringens enterotoxin C-terminal domain (d2quoa_). This provides a structural bridge to the Cry C-terminal family containing Cry3A; the annotation is not a direct ColG–Cry3A pairwise measurement. Supporting API comparisons for ColG’s near-identical chain-cluster representative 1nqjA report FATCAT matches to 2quo (initial RMSD 2.49 Å, P=1.4×10⁻⁶) and Cry4Ba’s C-terminal domain (2.52 Å, P=0.00395), despite low sequence identities in those structural alignments. These measurements belong to 1nqjA, not directly to 1nqd; the requested 1nqdA comparison returned no stored hits.

Functionally, these are compatible extracellular recognition modules: ColG’s domain binds collagen, Cry C-terminal domains contribute to receptor recognition and specificity, and the bridging enterotoxin domain binds claudin-4. Such binding roles support the evolutionary interpretation alongside structural correspondence, but do not independently prove ancestry or identical ligand specificity. The 1nqd domain is an accessory collagen-binding domain, not the collagenase catalytic domain. Neither collagenolysis, insecticidal activity, collagen binding, nor galactose binding can be transferred between these proteins solely from superfamily membership. A shared core can guide structural comparison, but binding loops, calcium-dependent features, and ligand contacts require separate validation.
